_comment: Nutrient definitions. ids = FoodData Central nutrient ids (first found wins). dv = FDA Daily Value for adults and children 4+ (21 CFR 101.9). rank = has a /foods-high-in/ page. dii = Dietary Inflammatory Index effect score (Shivappa et al. 2014); dii_ref = reference daily amount used to scale (FDA DV where one exists, else the DII global mean intake).

nutrients.name: Protein
nutrients.about: Protein supplies the amino acids used to build and repair muscle, skin, enzymes and hormones. The Daily Value is 50 g; needs rise with body weight, age and training.

nutrients.name: Fiber
nutrients.about: Dietary fiber is the part of plant foods that is not digested. It supports regular digestion, feeds gut bacteria and helps moderate blood sugar and cholesterol. The Daily Value is 28 g; most people get about half that.

nutrients.name: Sugars
nutrients.about: Total sugars include both the sugars naturally present in fruit, milk and vegetables and any added sugars. USDA SR Legacy does not separate added sugars, so this list ranks by total sugars; whole foods with the least are listed first.

nutrients.name: Monounsaturated fat
nutrients.about: Monounsaturated fats, the main fat in olive oil, avocados and most nuts, are associated with better blood lipid profiles when they replace saturated fat. There is no Daily Value; values here are grams per serving.

nutrients.name: Polyunsaturated fat
nutrients.about: Polyunsaturated fats include the essential omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids the body cannot make. Seeds, nuts, vegetable oils and fatty fish are the richest sources. There is no Daily Value; values here are grams per serving.

nutrients.name: Omega-3 (ALA+EPA+DHA)
nutrients.about: Omega-3 fatty acids: ALA from plant foods (flax, chia, walnuts) and EPA and DHA from fish and seafood. The Adequate Intake for ALA is 1.6 g a day for men and 1.1 g for women; there is no FDA Daily Value, so no %DV is shown.

nutrients.name: Sodium
nutrients.about: Sodium is essential in small amounts but most diets contain far more than the 2,300 mg Daily Value, mainly from processed and restaurant food. Whole foods are naturally low in sodium.

nutrients.name: Calcium
nutrients.about: Calcium builds bone and teeth and is needed for muscle contraction and nerve signalling. The Daily Value is 1,300 mg. Dairy, canned fish with bones, tofu set with calcium and leafy greens are the main food sources.

nutrients.name: Iron
nutrients.about: Iron carries oxygen in haemoglobin. The Daily Value is 18 mg. Heme iron from meat, fish and poultry is absorbed far better than non-heme iron from plants; vitamin C eaten at the same meal improves plant-iron absorption.

nutrients.name: Magnesium
nutrients.about: Magnesium takes part in more than 300 enzyme reactions, including energy production, muscle and nerve function and blood pressure regulation. The Daily Value is 420 mg. Seeds, nuts, legumes, whole grains and leafy greens are the richest sources.

nutrients.name: Phosphorus
nutrients.about: Phosphorus is a component of bone, cell membranes and DNA. The Daily Value is 1,250 mg. Deficiency is rare; people with kidney disease may need to limit it.

nutrients.name: Potassium
nutrients.about: Potassium is an electrolyte that helps regulate fluid balance, nerve signals and muscle contractions, and a higher intake is linked to lower blood pressure. The Daily Value is 4,700 mg, which most people do not reach. Beans, potatoes, leafy greens, fish, dairy and fruit are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Zinc
nutrients.about: Zinc supports immune function, wound healing, taste and smell, and protein and DNA synthesis. The Daily Value is 11 mg. Oysters, red meat, poultry, beans, nuts and whole grains are good sources; zinc from plants is less well absorbed.

nutrients.name: Copper
nutrients.about: Copper is needed for iron metabolism, energy production, connective tissue and the nervous system. The Daily Value is 0.9 mg. Shellfish, organ meats, nuts, seeds, chocolate and whole grains are rich sources.

nutrients.name: Manganese
nutrients.about: Manganese is a cofactor for enzymes involved in metabolism, bone formation and antioxidant defence. The Daily Value is 2.3 mg. Whole grains, nuts, legumes, leafy vegetables and tea are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Selenium
nutrients.about: Selenium is part of antioxidant enzymes and is needed for thyroid hormone metabolism. The Daily Value is 55 µg. Brazil nuts, seafood, meat, eggs and grains are the main sources; one Brazil nut can exceed the DV.

nutrients.name: Vitamin C
nutrients.about: Vitamin C is an antioxidant needed to make collagen and to absorb plant iron. The Daily Value is 90 mg. Peppers, citrus, berries, kiwifruit and cruciferous vegetables are the richest sources; cooking in water reduces it.

nutrients.name: Thiamin (B1)
nutrients.about: Thiamin (vitamin B1) helps convert carbohydrate into energy and supports nerve function. The Daily Value is 1.2 mg. Pork, fish, legumes, seeds and whole or enriched grains are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Riboflavin (B2)
nutrients.about: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is needed for energy production and the metabolism of fats, drugs and steroids. The Daily Value is 1.3 mg. Dairy, eggs, organ meats, lean meat, almonds and mushrooms are good sources.

nutrients.name: Niacin (B3)
nutrients.about: Niacin (vitamin B3) is used by hundreds of enzymes in energy metabolism and DNA repair. The Daily Value is 16 mg NE. Poultry, fish, meat, peanuts and whole grains are the richest sources.

nutrients.name: Vitamin B6
nutrients.about: Vitamin B6 is involved in amino acid metabolism, red blood cell formation and immune function. The Daily Value is 1.7 mg. Fish, poultry, potatoes, bananas, chickpeas and fortified cereals are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Folate (DFE)
nutrients.about: Folate (vitamin B9) is needed for DNA synthesis and cell division, and is especially important before and during pregnancy. The Daily Value is 400 µg DFE. Legumes, leafy greens, asparagus, liver and fortified grains are the richest sources.

nutrients.name: Vitamin B12
nutrients.about: Vitamin B12 is needed for red blood cells, nerve function and DNA synthesis. The Daily Value is 2.4 µg. It occurs naturally only in animal foods (shellfish, fish, meat, eggs, dairy); vegans need fortified foods or supplements.

nutrients.name: Vitamin A (RAE)
nutrients.about: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function and cell growth. The Daily Value is 900 µg RAE (retinol activity equivalents), which counts both preformed vitamin A from animal foods and carotenoids from orange and dark-green vegetables.

nutrients.name: Vitamin E
nutrients.about: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes. The Daily Value is 15 mg. Sunflower seeds, almonds, hazelnuts, vegetable oils and leafy greens are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Vitamin D
nutrients.about: Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium and for bone, muscle and immune health. The Daily Value is 20 µg (800 IU). Few foods contain much: fatty fish, fish liver oil, egg yolks, UV-exposed mushrooms and fortified milk and cereal.

nutrients.name: Vitamin K
nutrients.about: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting and bone metabolism. The Daily Value is 120 µg. Leafy greens (kale, spinach, collards), broccoli and Brussels sprouts contain very large amounts. People on warfarin should keep intake consistent.

nutrients.name: Choline
nutrients.about: Choline is needed for cell membranes, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and fat transport from the liver. The Daily Value is 550 mg. Eggs, liver, meat, fish, soybeans and cruciferous vegetables are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Beta-carotene
nutrients.about: Beta-carotene is the orange plant pigment the body converts to vitamin A, and an antioxidant in its own right. There is no Daily Value. Sweet potatoes, carrots, pumpkin, leafy greens and cantaloupe are the richest sources.

nutrients.name: Lycopene
nutrients.about: Lycopene is the red carotenoid in tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit and guava. It is an antioxidant studied for heart and prostate health. There is no Daily Value; values are micrograms per serving. Cooked tomato products supply far more than raw.

nutrients.name: Lutein + zeaxanthin
nutrients.about: Lutein and zeaxanthin are the carotenoids concentrated in the retina and studied for eye health. There is no Daily Value; studies commonly use 6 to 10 mg a day. Kale, spinach, other dark greens, egg yolks and corn are the main sources.

nutrients.name: Caffeine
nutrients.about: Caffeine is a stimulant found in coffee, tea, cocoa and energy drinks. There is no Daily Value; the FDA cites 400 mg a day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects in healthy adults. Values are milligrams per serving.
